title: Will the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit Really Be a Boon for Public Schools?
author: Mike Petrilli
summary: Petrilli examines whether the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, a voucher-like provision in the One Big Beautiful Bill launching in January, could become a funding stream for public school districts rather than just private-school choice, centering on Marguerite Roza's proposal for districts to bundle non-required services (field trips, tutoring, clubs) into a fee that scholarship-granting organizations could cover for every enrolled student via payroll-deduction contributions from employers. Petrilli walks through the objections from school-choice advocates (that this could crowd out a pluralistic provider market) and from critics like Peter Greene (that it undermines public schools' 'public mission'), while noting his own skepticism is narrower: he doubts the maneuver matches the law's intent, since the FSTC is explicitly a scholarship mechanism meant to go to individual students and families, not institutions. He recounts a personal anecdote about an Idaho bar-closing-time loophole to illustrate that legislative intent and legal text can diverge, concluding that if Treasury doesn't move to stop the district-fee maneuver, it will likely spread regardless of whether lawmakers intended it. The piece also surveys wider debates about Democratic strategy on school choice, citing mixed electoral evidence on whether opposing or embracing choice better serves candidates.
points: Roza's 'K12-plus plan' proposal — a nominal $800 district fee that virtually no family actually pays out of pocket because scholarship-granting organizations cover it via payroll-deducted employer contributions — describes a specific financial mechanism for redirecting FSTC dollars into district budgets.

Petrilli's core objection — that scholarships are legally meant to go 'directly to students,' not institutions — identifies a textual tension in Roza's proposal even though he concedes 'intent is irrelevant when the language is clear,' illustrating how legislative loopholes can survive despite not matching drafters' intent.

The Idaho tequila-shot anecdote is used as a concrete analogy for how legislative language can inadvertently permit outcomes lawmakers never intended, directly supporting the piece's argument that the FSTC district-fee maneuver may proceed regardless of intent if the statutory language allows it.

The electoral evidence cited on both sides — opposition to vouchers helping Democrats in several statehouse flips, but school-choice support outperforming among undecided Democratic primary voters in the Wisconsin governor's race — shows the piece resisting a simple partisan conclusion about voucher politics.
quotes: One of the big questions regarding the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit-the voucher-like provision in President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill that launches in January-is whether it could become a cash cow for public schools.

Our proposal: Districts set a fixed fee for access to a bundle of services. Imagine the district offers an $800 "K12-plus plan" that provides access to stuff like field trips, tutoring, homework help, assemblies, clubs or other services not required in the state's definition of required public education.
No scholarships are awarded to schools. Scholarships must be given directly to students, whose parents have the authority to receive and apply those funds for the benefit of the student's education.

The language of a new law inadvertently allowed for a later cutoff time for hard liquor sales than for beer. I'm sure that wasn't what most Idaho lawmakers "intended," but the law was ruled legit, and put into practice until revised a year later.
None of this means money will automatically flow to districts. Districts that want it will have to go after it. Some may choose not to. But it's not illegal.

Opposition to school vouchers turns out to have been a consistent, and underappreciated, ingredient in recent special elections in which Democrats have flipped Statehouse seats in Florida, Iowa, New Hampshire, and Georgia.
